Just look at you two, making plans like a couple of pensioners. I'll tell you what will happen: it will rain on Saturday, it will be sunny on Sunday and you'll miss the train back.

"voi" = vo-i (one syllable, like "boy"), "vei" = ve-i (like "vay"), "va" = va. They are unstressed: the stress falls on the verb: voi MER-ge.
In fast speech, "o să" is pronounced almost "o s": "o s-ajungem", "o s-o vezi".
It joins the verb: "am să-ți scriu" (no pause).
It is formed with the auxiliary "a vrea" (forms voi, vei, va…) + the infinitive without "a".
Reflexive and short pronouns come before: mă voi întoarce, te voi suna, o vom vizita.
Romanian has three forms of the future. The meaning is the same; the style differs.
speech; shows an intention, a promise
With "o să", the verb is in the subjunctive: o să merg, o să mergi, o să meargă, o să mergem, o să mergeți, o să meargă. The "o" never changes.
With "am să", "am" changes (am, ai, are, avem, aveți, au): am să vin, ai să vezi, are să plouă.
"Peste" + time = after a period (future): "Vin peste o oră." (I'll come in an hour.) "În" + time = within the period: "Termin în două ore." (I'll finish within two hours.)
For a real condition in the future, put the present after "dacă" and the future in the main clause.
If you have time, I'll show you the city.
If we miss the train, we'll take the bus.
Don't put the future after "dacă" in this kind of sentence: "Dacă va ploua…" is possible but sounds formal. Natural: "Dacă plouă…".
5. The present for the future too
As in many languages, the present is often used for fixed plans, especially with a time expression.
On Saturday I'm playing in Sibiu.
I'm coming to your place tonight.
Predictions (what you think will happen) are usually made with the future: "Va ploua." "O să-ți placă."
Tomorrow I will go to Sibiu.
We will leave on Saturday morning.
On Sunday it will be sunny.

Mrs Pop has many talents. She makes the best cozonac in the neighbourhood. She knows all of Eminescu's poems by heart. And she reads coffee grounds. About this last talent, Radu says it's "superstition". I say Mrs Pop has never been wrong.

On Friday morning at seven, the kitchen smelled of Turkish coffee. Mrs Pop made it in the copper coffee pot, the way her mother used to make it in Bistrița. She poured it into small white cups with blue flowers.
"Drink slowly," she told Nora. "And don't drink the grounds. When you finish, turn the cup upside down on the saucer and think of a question."

Nora drank slowly. Then she turned the cup over, closed her eyes and thought of something. She didn't say what. But I, sitting on the windowsill, saw her glance for a second at the door Radu had gone out through.
After five minutes, Mrs Pop picked up the cup, put on her glasses and looked inside very seriously, like a doctor reading an X-ray.
"Aha," she said. "I see a road. A long road, with rails. You will travel south, towards the mountains."
"I knew that already," laughed Nora. "We're going to Sibiu."
"Quiet, please. The coffee is talking, not you." Mrs Pop turned the cup a little. "Here is a cloud. It will rain. But look, after the cloud, a sun. The second day will be beautiful."
"I see an instrument. Long, slender, with strings." Mrs Pop raised an eyebrow. "And next to the instrument, a heart. It isn't very big. Yet. But it will grow."
Nora went red to the ears. I pretended to be asleep, so as not to embarrass her further.
"There's something else here, at the edge," Mrs Pop went on. "An envelope. A letter that will come from far away, from someone in the family. Someone young. And I see snow. Lots of snow."
"Elin!" exclaimed Nora. "My sister promised she would come at Christmas! But she hasn't confirmed yet."
"She will confirm," said Mrs Pop, sure of herself. "And one more thing: a clock." She looked more closely. "A clock showing the wrong time. You will run. You will run a lot."
"Will we miss the train?" asked Nora, worried.
Mrs Pop put the cup down and took off her glasses. "Coffee doesn't tell everything, my dear. It only tells what can be. The rest depends on you."
At that moment Radu came in, his hair wet from the shower. "Good morning! What are you doing? Superstitions again, Grandma?"
"No, my dear. Meteorology." And she poured him a coffee too.

Radu drank his coffee in a single gulp, as usual, and turned his cup over on the saucer too, "just for a laugh". Mrs Pop looked inside and smiled mysteriously. "What do you see, Grandma?" "I see a young man who will have to learn to wait. And to stop drinking his coffee so fast." Radu laughed, but didn't ask anything else.

An hour later, Nora's phone vibrated. It was a message from Elin: "I've bought the ticket! I arrive on 20 December. Let there be snow, please!" Nora looked at Mrs Pop. Mrs Pop shrugged and went on with her cozonac. I wasn't surprised at all. I told you: she has never been wrong.
